name: Methyltestosterone

lead: Methyltestosterone is one of the earliest orally active forms of testosterone. It has been used for male hypogonadism, in women in combination with estrogens for menopausal symptoms, and in hereditary angioedema. It is also a prohibited substance in sport.

For looksmaxxing purposes it has little documented use in the sources reviewed: no trial has tested it for muscle or facial appearance, and no community threads about it were found. The most relevant human study is a 1993 NIH trial in healthy men that measured mood and behavior effects.

paras: It is testosterone with a methyl group at the 17-alpha position, which allows oral dosing and raises the risk of liver effects. It acts on the androgen receptor; in human neurons it was shown to protect against apoptosis in vitro.[1][2]

Reported risks include virilization in women, liver toxicity, mood changes and a drug interaction with cyclosporine.[1][3] In the 1993 NIH trial, healthy men given methyltestosterone for two weeks were assessed for acute mood and behavioral effects.[4] Combination estrogen-methyltestosterone tablets carry a boxed warning about endometrial cancer risk and are Pregnancy Category X.[5]

lead: Methyltestosterone is a synthetic androgen, a 17-alpha-methyl derivative of testosterone that can be taken by mouth. It has been used to treat male hypogonadism, and in women as part of menopausal hormone therapy, usually combined with esterified estrogens.[1][2][3]

Controlled trials have tested it in hereditary angioedema, where in a double-blind study of four patients it was associated with fewer attacks, and in menopausal women, where added methyltestosterone improved one test of attention but showed no net change in overall outcome score.[4][5] A 1993 NIH double-blind crossover trial examined the acute effects of the drug on mood and behavior in 20 healthy men.[6]

No published study located has tested methyltestosterone for muscle, skin, face or other cosmetic outcomes in healthy people, and no community discussion of the compound was found among the forum sources reviewed.
infobox: Male hypogonadism; menopausal symptoms (with estrogens); hereditary angioedema
Prescription drug; controlled and prohibited in sport

paras: In men, methyltestosterone is an oral option for testosterone replacement; reviews of hypogonadism therapy discuss oral and alternative androgens.[1] Grokipedia describes use in primary and secondary hypogonadism, delayed puberty and, in women, palliation of advanced breast cancer, postpartum breast engorgement and menopausal symptoms.[7]

In women, androgen therapy has been used mainly to improve sexual function after menopause, and reviews discuss testosterone's role in female sexuality and well-being and the uncertain clinical definition of deficiency.[2][8] A US-labelled combination of esterified estrogens and methyltestosterone is indicated for moderate to severe vasomotor symptoms not improved by estrogens alone.[3] Randomized studies in postmenopausal women examined vasodilator effects, circulating hormone levels, stress cardiovascular responses and bone density with combined estrogen-androgen therapy.[9][10][11][12]
A double-blind trial found methyltestosterone effective in preventing hereditary angioedema attacks.[4]

Grokipedia states that methyltestosterone is misused by athletes and bodybuilders for strength and muscle and is prohibited by WADA, but gives no study quantifying the effect on appearance.[7] No trial in the sources tested it for physique or facial outcomes, and no looksmaxxing community threads were identified.

Randomized studies include a double-blind trial in four hereditary angioedema patients, an 8-week crossover trial adding methyltestosterone to estrogen in menopausal women, further trials of combined estrogen-androgen therapy in postmenopausal women, and a 2-week NIH placebo-controlled crossover trial of mood and behavior in 20 healthy men.[4][5][9][10][11][6] Registered trials identified concern testosterone undecanoate and other products, not methyltestosterone. No trial has examined appearance outcomes.

In hereditary angioedema, 10 mg daily in a double-blind study of four patients was associated with 4 attacks over 46 cumulative months versus 19 episodes over 11.8 months on placebo.[4] In menopausal women already on estrogen, adding methyltestosterone for eight weeks significantly improved a complex attention test but not other tests, and the overall score did not change on average.[5]

The 1993 NIH trial studied mood and behavioral effects of methyltestosterone in healthy male volunteers over two weeks.[6] A 1964 report described iatrogenic precocious pubescence, and a 1991 case report described a cyclosporine-methyltestosterone interaction.[13][14] The label of the estrogen-methyltestosterone combination carries a boxed warning on endometrial carcinoma, is Pregnancy Category X, and lists adverse effects associated with estrogens, including thromboembolism and gallbladder disease.[3] Grokipedia lists virilization in women, liver toxicity, cardiovascular issues and mood alterations.[7]

Methyltestosterone is an androgen-receptor agonist whose 17-alpha methyl group aids oral bioavailability. In a laboratory study, testosterone, methyltestosterone and epitestosterone at physiological concentrations protected human primary neurons from serum-deprivation-induced apoptosis via the androgen receptor.[15]

Methyltestosterone is widely used in aquaculture research to produce all-male fish stocks, and studies in zebrafish, flounder and fathead minnow describe its effects on gonad development and on aromatase expression; it has also been measured as an environmental steroid in wastewater.[16][17][18][19] These studies concern animals and the environment, not human appearance.
